[MUJAHID:v1p273/r1] MUJAHID, d. 104 · مجاهد | reports | A person among the polytheists may come to hear the message and revelation; he is safe until he hears God's speech and is then escorted to the place he came from.
[MUQATIL:9:6-10/r1] MUQATIL, d. 150 · author | holds | If a Meccan polytheist seeks protection after fifty days, the Prophet must secure him from killing, let him hear the Quran, and return him safely if he refuses it; should he later fight and be captured, he may be killed.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r1] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | A bare accusative can replace an understood verb when context makes the action clear: seeing a beating, one says زيدا to mean direct the action at Zayd.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r10] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Accusatives such as زيدا وعمرا can stand for an understood ضرب, and proverbs similarly omit commands: أمر مبكياتك and الظباء على البقر mean follow or leave the relevant things.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r2] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Repeated accusatives such as الأسد الأسد or الجدار الجدار are warnings meaning beware or do not approach; the explicit caution verb may also be stated.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r3] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | The warning طريق الطريق means clear or leave the road; one cannot elide تنح عن الطريق because a preposition-governed phrase is bound to its preposition.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r4] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · جرير | reports | Jarīr’s خل الطريق البيت shows the transitive command used for clearing the road, supporting the rule against omitting a preposition with its governed noun.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r5] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | An omitted command cannot target an absent third person through an intermediary: a hearer would mistake the bare accusative for a direct order addressed to them.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r6] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | holds | Arabic conventional phrases license omitted verbs when their intended wording is familiar, as in اللهم ضبعا وذئبا, meaning place a hyena and wolf among the flock.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r7] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | Sībawayh reports an Arab reply to a complaint about a spoiled place: the children were responsible, stated elliptically to avoid blame.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r8] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · author | reports | A trusted source reports an Arab identifying a water-holding place with بلى وجاذا, understood as فأعرف بها وجاذا.
[SIBAWAYH:وذلكقولكزيداوعمراورأسه|وذلكأنكرأيترجلايضربأويشتمأويقتل#99/r9] SIBAWAYH, d. 180 · المسكين | reports | The poet al-Miskīn’s أخال أخاك line implies الزم أخاك, illustrating an omitted command recoverable from context.
[FARRA:v1p421/r1] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The protection command requires returning the polytheist to his place of safety.
[FARRA:v1p421/r2] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | The conditional verb remains jussive though أحد separates إن from it; إن uniquely permits such separation because it is a particle rather than a noun.
[FARRA:v1p421/r3] FARRA, d. 207 · author | holds | Other intervening nominative or accusative words are likewise possible with إن; the cited verse and poetic line illustrate this looseness. | mentions 4:176

[FARRA:v1p421/r6] FARRA, d. 207 · الكسائي | reports | Al-Kisāʾī cites a poem in which الخير appears accusative after a jussive conditional, but al-Farrāʾ parses it as an adjective of الأيام and reads تعقب as feminine.

[IBNHISHAM:v2p543#2/r1] IBNHISHAM, d. 213 · author | holds | Ibn Hisham ties the revelation of Bara'a to ending the general pact with polytheists, the Prophet's special tribal agreements, the Tabuk absentees, and hypocrites whose hidden beliefs the sūra exposed.
[IBNHISHAM:v2p543#2/r6] IBNHISHAM, d. 213 · author | holds | Anyone among those ordered to be fought who seeks protection must receive it until hearing God's speech, then be escorted to safety because they are ignorant.

[AKHFASH:v1p354/r6] AKHFASH, d. 215 · author | holds | The verse can likewise be parsed with أحد raised by an understood verb.

[TAB-FULL:v11p348/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | rejects | Al-Tabari rejects abrogation: no proof establishes an earlier universal duty to kill every polytheist that a later permission to pardon or ransom could cancel.
[TAB-FULL:v11p348/r5] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Killing, release without payment, and ransom were all part of the Prophet’s practice from Badr; the command thus leaves these options available rather than requiring killing in every case.

[TAB-FULL:v1p8#2/r2] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | People differ in expressive capacity, from accomplished speakers to those unable to articulate what is in their hearts.
[TAB-FULL:v1p8#2/r3] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | The highest rank of expression belongs to one who conveys intent most clearly and brings it closest to the listener’s understanding.
[TAB-FULL:v1p8#2/r4] TAB-FULL, d. 310 · author | holds | Al-Ṭabarī cites 43:18 to show the superiority of eloquent people over the mute and inarticulate rests on their ability to express themselves. | mentions 43:18
